blogs.title: “We Almost Need to Come Inside”: Semantics, Voluntariness, and Third-Party Consent in Domestic-Violence Responses
blogs.description: This post examines the Seventh Circuit’s treatment of voluntariness where an officer told a domestic-violence complainant, “I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside.” It parses the line between a request and an assertion of authority under Bumper and Hicks, and situates the analysis within third-party consent doctrine (Matlock) and Randolph/Fernandez co-occupant cases. The piece assesses how tone, prior refusal, and the totality-of-circumstances framework (including the absence of an advisement of the right to refuse) guided the court’s conclusion that consent was voluntary, and what that means for police phrasing during knock-and-talks in sensitive domestic settings.

blogs.title: Defining the “Scope” in Welfare Checks: From Entry to Canvass to Warrant
blogs.description: Focusing on Florida v. Jimeno’s objective-reasonableness test, this post explores how the court linked the expressed purpose—checking on children’s safety—to the officers’ subsequent actions: entering, canvassing rooms, locating the husband, briefly patting him down, and interviewing the children. It addresses the uneasy border between consent-based welfare checks and investigative steps, the shadow of Buie protective-sweep principles even when not cited, and best practices for cabining scope in consent entries to avoid suppression while still enabling effective response to domestic-violence calls.

blogs.title: When Video “Evaporates” Disputes: Body Cameras, Clear Error, and the Appellate Insulation of Consent Findings
blogs.description: This post analyzes the opinion’s heavy reliance on bodycam footage under Scott v. Harris and Norville and how that, combined with the clear-error standard, fortified the district court’s consent and scope determinations. It discusses strategic implications for suppression litigation—what arguments remain viable when video captures tone and sequence; how defense and government frame voluntariness under video; and whether the growing centrality of video evidence subtly shifts trial-level factfinding power in Fourth Amendment disputes.

blogs.title: The Roads Not Taken: Exigent Circumstances and Inevitable Discovery in Domestic-Violence Entries
blogs.description: Although the panel affirmed on consent, it explicitly sidestepped exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery. This post explores how the emergency-aid and exigency doctrines could have applied given 911 reports of threats to kill, the late hour, and momentary uncertainty about children’s safety. It evaluates the strategic choice to rest on consent, the risk of narrowing exigency precedents by non-use, and what guidance departments should draw for future domestic-violence responses when consent is equivocal or refused.
